docs.title: FutureQ
docs.text:
A high-performance, distributed delayed-message queue broker written in Go.

FutureQ lets producers publish messages with a relative delay and guarantees reliable dispatch to consumers when the delay expires. It combines durable embedded storage, Raft-based replication, and bidirectional gRPC streaming into a single, easy-to-operate binary.

Get started GitHub repository Protocol definition

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• ⏱ Delayed messaging — enqueue a message with a delay_ms; it becomes visible to consumers only after the delay expires. Optional per-message ttl_ms discards messages nobody consumed.
  • 💾 Durable storage — disk-backed by Pebble (CockroachDB's LSM store) with a time-optimized 24-byte key schema, a pure in-memory mode, and an alternative bbolt engine.
  • 🔀 High availability — multi-node replication via Dragonboat (multi-group Raft): an event shard for messages plus a metadata group for cluster topology.
  • ➕ Dynamic membership — nodes join and leave a running cluster over gRPC (JoinCluster / LeaveCluster) with catch-up before voting. No static bootstrap list needed after the first node.
  • 👥 Consumer groups & topics — topic-based routing with fan-out across groups and round-robin dispatch within a group. "Universal" consumers (no group) each receive every message.
  • ✅ At-least-once delivery — in-flight tracking with automatic re-dispatch of unacknowledged messages; batched deletes (a single Raft proposal per batch) amortize LSM tombstone costs.
  • ⚙️ Tunable durability — publish acknowledgements at three levels: quorum commit, leader-local persistence (fast path), or fire-and-forget — with a broker-side minimum enforced by policy.
  • 📈 Observability — Prometheus metrics endpoint and structured logging (zap) out of the box.

docs.title: Technology stack
docs.text: Concern Choice Language Go 1.27.1 Storage Pebble (LSM tree) · bbolt (alternative) · in-memory Consensus Dragonboat v4 (multi-group Raft) Transport gRPC (bidirectional streaming) Metrics Prometheus Protocol futureq-io/protocol (Protobuf, v0.2.0)

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
┌──────────────┐   PublishStream   ┌──────────────────────────┐
                │  Producer    │ ─────────────────▶│                          │
                └──────────────┘                   │        FutureQ Node       │
                                                   │                          │
                ┌──────────────┐   Subscribe       │  ┌────────────────────┐  │
                │  Consumer    │ ◀──────────────── │  │ gRPC API (8443)    │  │
                └──────────────┘                   │  └─────────┬──────────┘  │
                                                   │            ▼             │
                ┌──────────────┐   Raft (50005)    │  ┌────────────────────┐  │
                │  Other Nodes │ ◀───────────────▶ │  │ Dispatcher / Hub   │  │
                └──────────────┘                   │  │ Deleter · Janitor  │  │
                                                   │  └─────────┬──────────┘  │
                ┌──────────────┐   Prometheus      │            ▼             │
                │  Metrics     │ ◀── (9090) ──────│  │ Pebble + Raft log    │  │
                └──────────────┘                   │  └────────────────────┘  │
                                                   └──────────────────────────┘
  • Writes go through Raft as one log entry per batch (or straight to Pebble in standalone mode) and are stored under time-bucketed keys for efficient expiry scans.
  • Reads are push-based: the dispatcher scans for due messages and routes them to connected consumers through a hub using a round-robin strategy per consumer group.
  • Acks are batched by a deleter and committed as a single Raft proposal, keeping write amplification low.

Delivery is at-least-once — consumers should be idempotent.

docs.title: gRPC API
docs.text: FutureQ speaks gRPC; protobuf definitions live in futureq-io/protocol (v0.2.0). The server registers three services: futureq.FutureQProducer, futureq.FutureQConsumer, and futureq.FutureQCluster.

docs.title: Services overview
docs.text: RPC Service Type Description PublishStream Producer bidi streaming Publish batches of delayed messages; receive per-batch acks Subscribe Consumer bidi streaming Receive messages for a topic/consumer group; ack over the same stream GetClusterInfo Cluster unary Cluster topology, leader and member metadata JoinCluster Cluster unary Add a node to the event shard and metadata group LeaveCluster Cluster unary Gracefully remove a node from the cluster JoinMetadata Cluster unary Add a non-voting observer to the metadata group (SDKs/brokers) LeaveMetadata Cluster unary Remove a metadata observer

docs.title: PublishStream
docs.text:
/futureq.FutureQProducer/PublishStream — bidi stream of PublishBatch → PublishBatchAck.

  • Each PublishBatch carries messages (topic, payload, delay_ms, ttl_ms, optional indexes) and an ack_level.
  • Exactly one PublishBatchAck{success, error_message} is sent per received batch — batch-level semantics: the batch fails atomically (no partial write) on negative delays/TTLs, a too-weak ack level, or non-leader contact in Raft mode. On failure the RPC-level gRPC status also carries the error.
  • An empty batch returns a default (unsuccessful) ack and performs no write.
  • Client half-close (EOF) ends the stream cleanly.
  • Ack levels: QUORUM (default; returns after Raft quorum commit), LEADER (returns after the leader durably persists the entry — see ack levels), NO_ACK (fire-and-forget). The broker's publish.minAckLevel floors what clients may request.
  • In Raft mode only the event-shard leader accepts writes; standalone always writes directly to storage with fsync.

docs.title: Subscribe
docs.text: /futureq.FutureQConsumer/Subscribe — bidi stream of ConsumerFrame → QueueMessage.

docs.title: Handshake
docs.text:
• The first frame must be ConsumerFrame{init: SubscribeInit{topic, group_id, read_from_replica}}.
  • Errors: non-init first frame → InvalidArgument; empty topic → InvalidArgument.
  • In Raft mode the node must be the event-shard leader → FailedPrecondition "node is not the cluster leader". Standalone accepts always. (read_from_replica is reserved for future follower reads and currently ignored.)

docs.title: After registration
docs.text:
• The broker assigns a UUID and registers the consumer with the hub (buffered channel, capacity 1024).
  • group_id semantics: empty = universal consumer (receives every message); non-empty = competing group (round-robin within the group, fan-out across groups).
  • Server → client frames are QueueMessage with delivery_tag — an opaque tag the client must echo back.
  • Client → server frames are AckRequest{success, delivery_tag}:
    • success = true (ACK): the message is queued for batched deletion and becomes non-re-dispatchable.
    • success = false (NACK): nothing is deleted; the message becomes re-dispatchable immediately.
  • Any ack frame also removes the in-flight entry for that consumer. Non-ack frames after handshake are logged and skipped.
  • Client EOF ends the stream cleanly; the consumer is unregistered and its in-flight keys dropped.

docs.title: GetClusterInfo
docs.text:
• Returns leader_node_id, leader_address, and the member list (node_id, address, is_leader).
  • Any node answers. On a standalone node → NotFound; before topology is available → Unavailable.
  • Node addresses prefer the registered gRPC address, falling back to the Raft address.

docs.title: JoinCluster
docs.text:
• Request: node_id, raft_address, grpc_address.
  • Must be sent to the leader (not forwarded). Runs add-non-voting → catch-up wait (30s) → promote-to-voter on both the event shard and the metadata group.
  • Failures are reported in JoinResponse{success, error_message} without failing the RPC status.

docs.title: LeaveCluster
docs.text: Removes the node from the event shard and then the metadata group (leader, same response conventions). Afterwards the node's local Raft data can be deleted.

docs.title: JoinMetadata / LeaveMetadata
docs.text: Add/remove a non-voting observer on the metadata group only — for client SDKs or new brokers that want live topology without participating in consensus.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Danger

The gRPC server is plaintext — no TLS and no authentication. All RPCs, including cluster membership mutations, are open on the configured listen address. Run it on a trusted network or in front of a TLS-terminating proxy.

Server tuning from config: maxConcurrentStreams (default 10), max message sizes (100KiB), keepalive (min 5s, permit-without-stream, idle 30s, max connection age 2m + 10s grace, ping 10s, timeout from api.grpc.keepaliveTimeout).

docs.title: Standalone vs. clustered
docs.text:
One binary, two operating modes, selected by cluster.enabled:

Standalone (enabled: false) Clustered (enabled: true) Writes Direct Pebble batch, fsynced per publish batch One Raft log entry per publish batch, applied by the on-disk state machine on every replica Deletes Direct storage batch DeleteBatchCmd proposed through Raft — replicated, so a new leader can't resurrect ACKed messages Dispatch Always Only on the event-shard leader Consume Always Only on the leader (client SDKs learn the leader's address from the metadata group) Membership — Event shard + metadata group (shard 0), joined over gRPC

docs.title: Write path
docs.text:
1. A producer sends a PublishBatch over the PublishStream bidi stream.
  2. The broker validates (no negative delays/TTLs; batch ack level ≥ broker minimum) and wraps each message into a serialized StoredMessage.
  3. The leader assigns each message a monotonic event ID (persisted across restarts), computes its time bucket from enqueue time + delay, and hashes the topic.
  4. Clustered mode: the whole batch becomes a single StoreBatchCmd Raft log entry; replicas apply it verbatim so keys converge. Standalone: one Pebble batch, committed with fsync.
  5. The message lands in storage under a 24-byte time-bucketed key (topicHash · bucket · eventID) plus optional secondary indexes.

docs.title: Read path
docs.text:
Reads are push-based — consumers never poll the broker:

  1. A consumer opens a Subscribe bidi stream with topic and group; the hub registers it.
  2. The dispatcher periodically scans only topics with active consumers for due buckets (a pure range scan that never touches future buckets).
  3. Due messages fan out through the hub: every consumer group gets one copy, round-robin within the group; universal consumers each get every message.
  4. Delivered messages become in-flight until ACKed; after inFlightTimeout they are re-dispatched (at-least-once).

docs.title: Delete path
docs.text:
1. Consumer ACKs carry the opaque delivery_tag (the raw storage key).
  2. The deleter accumulates keys and flushes them every deleteBatchInterval as one batched delete — a single Raft proposal in clustered mode — amortizing LSM tombstone costs.
  3. Failed delete batches are retried on the next flush.

docs.title: Components
docs.text: Component Location Role gRPC server internal/api/grpc Producer, consumer, and cluster services; plaintext gRPC with keepalive and size limits from config Dispatcher internal/dispatcher Due-bucket scanning, in-flight tracking, leader gating Hub internal/dispatcher Consumer registry; universal fan-out + round-robin per group Deleter internal/dispatcher Batched deletes with pluggable backend (Raft proposal or direct storage) TTL janitor internal/dispatcher Periodic full-DB sweep for expired unconsumed messages Event state machine internal/raft/event Dragonboat on-disk state machine applying StoreBatchCmd/DeleteBatchCmd to Pebble Metadata group pkg/raft/metadata Replicated cluster topology + nodeID→gRPC-address registry (shard 0) Leader persistence internal/raft/leaderpersist LogDB decorator enabling leader-ack publishes Event repository internal/repository Monotonic ID assignment, key construction, secondary indexes Storage engines internal/storage Pebble and bbolt behind a common ordered-key contract Config internal/config YAML + env loading with full validation Metrics internal/metrics Prometheus HTTP endpoint (started before Raft, for probes) App wiring internal/app Storage init, Raft lifecycle, graceful shutdown

docs.title: CLI
docs.text: The binary is built with Cobra. Both subcommands share the persistent --config / -c flag.

docs.title: futureq start
docs.text:
futureq start [-c config.yaml] [--join seed:8443 ...]
  • Loads and validates the config (file + FUTUREQ_* env).
  • Initializes storage and the event repository.
  • --join (repeatable) overrides cluster.joinSeeds for this start. Used only on a fresh start (no local Raft data); restarts skip the join flow.
  • Builds the hub, deleter (Raft delete backend in clustered mode, direct backend in standalone), and TTL janitor.
  • Starts the Prometheus metrics server before Raft, then the Raft groups (if enabled), then the gRPC server.
  • Waits for SIGTERM/SIGINT; shuts down gracefully with a 10s window — components are WaitGroup-tracked; gRPC gets GracefulStop with a hard Stop fallback if the deadline expires.

docs.title: futureq leave
docs.text:
futureq leave --seed <host:8443> [-c config.yaml]
  • Calls LeaveCluster on the seed with the configured cluster.nodeId (30s timeout).
  • --seed is required; fails if clustering is disabled or the RPC fails.
  • After a successful leave, the node's local Raft data directory can be deleted.

docs.title: Exit codes
docs.text: Configuration validation errors, failed joins, and failed leaves exit non-zero with a log message; start exits 0 after a clean signal-triggered shutdown.

docs.title: Raft clustering
docs.text: Replication is built on Dragonboat v4 (multi-group Raft). Each clustered node participates in two Raft groups.

docs.title: Two Raft groups
docs.text:
Event shard Metadata shard Shard ID cluster.shardId (default 1) 0 (fixed, exported from pkg/raft/metadata) State machine EventStateMachine — on-disk (IOnDiskStateMachine) over the same Pebble DB MetadataStateMachine — in-memory; rebuilt from the log on restart Holds All messages, indexes, and metadata keys Per-shard topology (leader, members, addresses) + nodeID→gRPC-address registry Raft settings Election RTT 10, heartbeat RTT 1, CheckQuorum; snapshot intervals from config Same timers; aggressive snapshots (every 5 entries) — state is tiny

Note

In clustered mode the Pebble WAL is disabled — the Raft log is the authoritative write-ahead log, and Dragonboat replays committed-but-unapplied entries on restart.

docs.title: Event-shard commands
docs.text:
Two binary commands (documented wire formats in internal/raft/event/commands.go), each big-endian, single-allocation marshal, zero-copy unmarshal:

Command Payload StoreBatchCmd (0) Per item: u64 id (leader-assigned event ID; replicas apply verbatim so keys converge) · u64 bucket · u64 topicHash · index entries · u32 len + pre-serialized StoredMessage. One publish batch = one log entry. DeleteBatchCmd (1) Count + fixed 24-byte message keys — used for ACK-driven deletes and TTL expirations.

Update applies all entries in a log batch into one Pebble batch (nothing partial on error), persists the max applied event ID and metadata/raft/applied-index, and fires the OnDeleteKeys hook so every replica clears dispatcher in-flight entries for deleted keys. Snapshots stream the whole DB as length-prefixed records; recovery clears the DB first and validates the applied index.

docs.title: Metadata group
docs.text: A metadata.Service registers as Dragonboat's Raft/system event listener. On leader or membership changes (ignoring shard 0 itself) it snapshots the shard membership into an UpdateTopologyCmd and proposes it to the metadata group with an ever-increasing epoch. Each node also proposes RegisterNodeAddrCmd(nodeID, api.grpc.advertise) at startup, retrying until the metadata group has a leader. The result: every node (and any SDK that joins as an observer) has a replicated view of the cluster topology, including the leader's client-facing gRPC address — that's what client SDKs dial.

docs.title: Joining (fresh node)
docs.text:
1. The fresh node (no local Raft data) dials each seed's gRPC address and calls JoinCluster with its node ID, Raft address, and gRPC address.
  2. The seed runs the three-step dance on both groups:
    1. SyncRequestAddNonVoting — join without affecting quorum;
    2. wait for catch-up (polling membership every 500ms, 30s deadline);
    3. SyncRequestAddReplica — promote to voter.
  3. The joining node starts its Raft groups in "join" mode; membership was registered via the RPC.

Warning

JoinCluster must reach the leader (membership ops fail on followers); the RPC is not forwarded. Clients should ask GetClusterInfo first or retry across seeds.

docs.title: Leaving
docs.text:
• futureq leave --seed <addr> (or a direct LeaveCluster RPC) removes the node's replica from the event shard and then the metadata group.
  • LeaveMetadata removes a metadata-group observer only.

docs.title: Restart
docs.text:
• If local Raft data exists (logdb-0/MANIFEST-000001), the node skips the join flow and starts as an existing member.
  • On ErrShardNotBootstrapped (e.g. stale data from an aborted bootstrap), the app wipes cluster.raft.dataDir so the next start retries cleanly instead of crash-looping.

docs.title: Leader persistence
docs.text: internal/raft/leaderpersist decorates Dragonboat's LogDB ("tan+leaderpersist"). After every successful SaveRaftState it hashes each persisted log entry's command and notifies the tracker, which closes registered waiter channels. This is the mechanism behind the leader ack level: a publisher is acknowledged once the leader has durably written the entry to its local Raft log — before quorum commit. Correlation is by command hash; in-flight payloads can't collide because batch commands embed monotonically increasing event IDs.

docs.title: Publish ack levels
docs.text:
Level Durability Mechanism ACK_LEVEL_QUORUM (default) Returns after majority commit SyncPropose bounded by publish.proposalTimeout (default 5s) ACK_LEVEL_LEADER Returns once the leader durably persisted the entry locally; followers replicate asynchronously Async propose + leaderpersist tracker wait. Can lose data on leader crash. ACK_LEVEL_NO_ACK Fire-and-forget; success means "submitted" only Async propose, no wait

The broker enforces a configurable floor: publish.minAckLevel (quorum | leader | noAck, default quorum). A batch requesting a level weaker than the floor is rejected with InvalidArgument. A missing/unknown level field counts as QUORUM.

docs.title: Restart & recovery
docs.text:
• Event IDs never regress: the last ID is persisted in the Pebble metadata keyspace and replicas observe applied IDs.
  • Committed-but-unapplied log entries are replayed on restart (Pebble WAL is off in clustered mode).
  • Snapshots restore the full DB (validated against the applied index); the metadata state machine rebuilds from its log.
  • ACKed messages can't be re-dispatched after failover because deletes are Raft-replicated.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text: Configuration is a YAML file passed via futureq start -c config.yaml. Every value is documented in config.example.yaml, which mirrors the built-in defaults. The config must carry configVersion: 1.

docs.title: Loading & precedence
docs.text:
Values are merged in this order (later wins):

  1. Built-in defaults — the default config serialized to YAML.
  2. Config file — merged key-by-key.
  3. Environment variables — via viper automatic env binding.

The binary uses viper.UnmarshalExact, so unknown keys in the file are rejected rather than silently ignored.

docs.title: Environment overrides
docs.text:
Every value can be overridden with the FUTUREQ_ prefix, dots replaced by underscores (dashes too):

export FUTUREQ_STORAGE_PEBBLE_DATADIR="/var/lib/futureq/data"
export FUTUREQ_OBSERVABILITY_LOGGING_LEVEL="debug"
export FUTUREQ_PUBLISH_MINACKLEVEL="leader"
export FUTUREQ_API_GRPC_LISTEN="0.0.0.0:8443"

Maps cannot come from a single env string, so FUTUREQ_CLUSTER_RAFT_INITIALMEMBERS is special-cased: its value is parsed as YAML, e.g.:

export FUTUREQ_CLUSTER_RAFT_INITIALMEMBERS='{1: "10.0.0.1:50005"}'

docs.title: api.grpc
docs.text: Key Default Description api.grpc.listen 0.0.0.0:8443 Address the gRPC server binds to. api.grpc.advertise "" Client-facing address registered in the cluster. Must be a non-wildcard address (no 0.0.0.0/::) when cluster.enabled. api.grpc.maxConcurrentStreams 10 gRPC MaxConcurrentStreams per connection. api.grpc.maxReceiveMessageSize 100KiB Max inbound message size. Sizes accept B/KiB/MiB/GiB units. api.grpc.maxSendMessageSize 100KiB Max outbound message size. api.grpc.keepaliveTimeout 5s Server keepalive timeout.

docs.title: cluster
docs.text: Key Default Description cluster.enabled false Enable Raft replication; false = standalone node writing directly to storage. cluster.nodeId 1 Unique Raft node ID. Must be nonzero when clustering is enabled. cluster.shardId 1 Event-shard ID. Must be nonzero. cluster.joinSeeds [] gRPC addresses of existing nodes to contact for JoinCluster. Mutually exclusive with initialMembers. cluster.raft.listen 0.0.0.0:50005 Dragonboat Raft listen address. cluster.raft.advertise "" Raft address advertised to peers. Non-wildcard when clustering. cluster.raft.dataDir ./raft-data Dragonboat LogDB / node-host data directory. cluster.raft.initialMembers {} Bootstrap map nodeId → raftAddress for a fresh cluster. If set, it must contain this node's own ID mapped to its advertise address. cluster.raft.rtt 200ms Estimated inter-node round-trip time driving Dragonboat's timers. Whole milliseconds, ≥1ms. cluster.raft.snapshotEntries 10000 Take a state-machine snapshot after this many applied log entries. cluster.raft.compactionOverhead 5000 Log entries retained above the snapshot index.

docs.title: storage
docs.text:
Key Default Description storage.engine pebble pebble (LSM) or bolt (single-file B+-tree). storage.payloadCacheSlots 4096 Shared payload freshness slots per DB, for both engines and standalone/Raft. Power of two from 64 to 1048576; requires restart. Larger counts reduce conservative cache invalidations from hash collisions. storage.payloadCacheHash fnv Slot hash: fnv (FNV-1a 64-bit) or xxhash64 (XXH64). Fixed when the DB opens; requires restart. Applies to both engines and standalone/Raft. storage.pebble.mode disk disk or memory (Pebble over an in-memory FS; nothing persists). storage.pebble.dataDir ./data Pebble data directory. storage.pebble.walEnabled true Pebble WAL toggle. Automatically disabled in memory mode and in clustered mode (the Raft log is the WAL); may only be set false explicitly for clustered disk nodes. storage.pebble.cacheSize 16MiB Block cache size. storage.pebble.memtableSize 64MiB Memtable size. storage.bolt.file ./data/futureq.db bbolt database file (engine bolt). storage.bolt.bucket futureq Single bbolt bucket holding the flat ordered keyspace.

For example, set storage.payloadCacheSlots: 16384 or FUTUREQ_STORAGE_PAYLOADCACHESLOTS=16384. This changes freshness tracking, not the number of cached messages or Pebble's block cache. At S slots the tracking arrays use approximately 12*S bytes per DB. Batches touching message keys allocate a bitmap of S/8 bytes (512 bytes at the default count), setting one bit per touched slot. Duplicate keys and collisions need no sorting. Each commit pass checks S/64 bitmap words and visits their set bits; metadata-only batches allocate no bitmap. There is no bitmap pool. At the maximum slot count, each payload batch allocates 128 KiB for its bitmap. Benchmark cache-hit rates and delivery latency before increasing the slot count substantially.

Set storage.payloadCacheHash: xxhash64 or FUTUREQ_STORAGE_PAYLOADCACHEHASH=xxhash64 to select XXH64. FNV remains the default; changing the hash changes collision patterns as well as hashing cost. Nodes may use different slot counts and algorithms because these settings affect only local freshness proofs, not stored keys, records, or the wire format. Wider hash output does not increase the number of freshness slots; XXH128 is not supported.

docs.title: publish
docs.text: Key Default Description publish.minAckLevel quorum Broker-wide minimum acknowledgement durability. One of quorum, leader, noAck. Publish batches requesting a weaker level are rejected with InvalidArgument. See ack levels. publish.proposalTimeout 5s Upper bound for each Raft propose / leader-ack wait. Must be positive.

docs.title: delivery
docs.text:
Key Default Description delivery.timeBucket 1ms Granularity of the key scheme's time buckets. 0 = raw-millisecond buckets (maximum precision). Otherwise must be ≥1ms. delivery.discoveryWorkers 2 Independent storage discovery workers, 1..16; at most one scan per topic. delivery.preloadScanIdleMaxInterval 100ms Maximum speculative idle scan backoff. 0 disables it; must be nonnegative. The effective limit is at least the poll interval. Payload mutations reset backoff; due repair cadence is unchanged. delivery.dispatchPollInterval 5ms Periodic live due-message scan interval, also used when preloading is enabled. delivery.preloadLookahead 0s How far ahead the scheduler scans for upcoming messages. Must be a nonnegative whole number of milliseconds. 0 disables preloading. delivery.preloadMaxMessages 512 Maximum retained/reserved full-message future entries across topics, 0..1048576. 0 disables future caching; bounded due delivery continues. Payload sizes determine memory use. delivery.inFlightTimeout 5s How long an unacknowledged delivery blocks redelivery; after it expires the message is re-dispatched (at-least-once). delivery.deleteBatchInterval 500ms How often the deleter flushes its batch of keys to delete (one Raft proposal per batch in clustered mode). delivery.ttlsweepInterval 60s How often the TTL janitor sweeps the whole database for expired messages.

All four intervals and the in-flight timeout must be greater than zero.

Preloading works in standalone and clustered mode. Configure it independently of preparation batch sizes and quorum reads:

delivery:
  preloadLookahead: 0s # opt-in trial: 100ms
  preloadMaxMessages: 512

The corresponding environment variables are FUTUREQ_DELIVERY_PRELOADLOOKAHEAD and FUTUREQ_DELIVERY_PRELOADMAXMESSAGES. Either setting can be zero to disable preloading. Increasing the lookahead or count does not change the scheduled due time, freeze recipients early, or bypass a delivery read barrier. See the full-message cache sizing and resource budget before retaining an existing large count: this cache now owns payload data.

docs.title: observability
docs.text: Key Default Description observability.logging.level info zap log level. observability.metrics.listen 0.0.0.0:9090 HTTP address exposing Prometheus metrics.

docs.title: Validation rules
docs.text:
• configVersion must be 1.
  • Advertised hosts may not be wildcard (0.0.0.0 / ::); listen addresses may.
  • When cluster.enabled: nodeId and shardId must be nonzero, and api.grpc.advertise / cluster.raft.advertise must be set to reachable addresses.
  • cluster.raft.initialMembers and cluster.joinSeeds are mutually exclusive.
  • If initialMembers is set, it must include this node's own ID mapped to its own Raft advertise address.
  • cluster.raft.rtt must be whole milliseconds ≥1ms.
  • Unknown publish.minAckLevel values fail startup.
  • storage.pebble.walEnabled: false is only legal for clustered disk nodes.

docs.title: Delivery pipeline
docs.text:
storage ──range scan──▶ Dispatcher ──▶ Hub ──▶ consumer channels
                         ▲                │
    ack ──────────────────┘──── Deleter ◀──┘   (delete batches → Raft/storage)
                                  ▲
 expired messages ────────────────┘  (TTL janitor full-DB sweep)

docs.title: Dispatcher
docs.text:
A timer-driven loop (delivery.dispatchPollInterval, default 5ms) scans topics with active local consumers. Each topic has at most one bounded preparation job, and a fixed worker pool limits outstanding work. Worker completions and hub wake signals also trigger scheduling. Clustered replicas filter candidates using the current committed ownership view and delivery permission.

The live due-message scan uses a snapshot and an independent cyclic cursor. Wrapping the cursor revisits older insertions, failed preparations, full consumer queues, NACKs, and timeout retries. Iterators close before preparation begins.

docs.title: Caching upcoming messages
docs.text:
Two bounded discovery workers load owned full-message data into per-topic heaps. The scheduler selects exact due times independently of scans and quorum work. delivery.preloadLookahead controls future discovery (default disabled; opt-in trial: 100 ms), and delivery.preloadMaxMessages bounds future messages across topics (default 512). A separate bounded due allowance keeps ordinary delivery working when either future setting is zero and when the future cache is full.

A timer wakes at eligible cached deadlines. Recipients are captured when due, using current ownership and epoch. Delivery workers prepare receipts, perform the post-preparation read barrier, validate payload versions, read current committed ACK state, recheck exact due time/TTL and enqueue through the existing Hub. Valid cached data avoids a second full-payload Get/decode in final delivery; uncertain/invalidated data uses a counted fresh-read fallback. Preparation still performs existence reads. The original permit and actual-send fences remain.

Due and future cursors are independent cyclic scan positions, never completion watermarks. Late arrivals, retries, rejected admission and stale results recover through due scans even without arrival hints. Failed jobs evict their payloads and retry after bounded backoff. Topic generations reject stale scan/delivery results after subscription changes. Storage batch invalidation covers deletion, replay, overwrite and snapshot replacement before old data can validate.

docs.title: Hub & consumer groups
docs.text:
Each consumer registers with a topic and a group and gets a UUID and a buffered channel (capacity 1024). Delivery semantics per topic:

Consumer kind group_id Behavior Grouped non-empty Competing: exactly one consumer in the group receives each message, chosen round-robin; the pointer rotates per group on every dispatch. Universal empty Fan-out: every universal consumer receives every message; they never compete with each other or with groups.

Different groups each get an independent copy of each message. Delivery to a channel is non-blocking: a slow consumer with a full channel is skipped for that message (with a warning) and, if no consumer in the topic accepted it, the message is simply not marked in-flight and is retried on the next pass.

docs.title: In-flight tracking & redelivery
docs.text:
• Queueing a message reserves its topic, group, and storage key across every member of that group. Universal consumers each retain their own independent in-flight tracking. Repeated scans cannot send a reserved message to another member of the same group.
  • Buffered attempts expire after delivery.inFlightTimeout (default 5s) if sending never starts. When the gRPC sender begins a valid attempt, it starts a fresh timeout for sending and acknowledgement, so queue waiting does not consume the ACK window.
  • An in-flight delivery blocks re-dispatch to its group until the timeout elapses — then the reservation is released and the message can be re-dispatched on the next pass, possibly to a different member.
  • Removal paths:
    • Consumer ACK persistence succeeds (only that recipient's tracking is released; failed batches retain tracking while they retry, subject to the normal timeout and disconnect behavior).
    • Consumer NACK (the gRPC handler releases the entry immediately, making the message re-dispatchable).
    • Consumer disconnect (the hub drops that consumer's in-flight keys instantly).
    • Batched delete applied through Raft (replicas clear their in-flight maps too).

docs.title: Deleter
docs.text:
• ACKs feed recipient completions into the deleter via TryMarkAcknowledged; explicit deletions and TTL expirations enqueue keys via MarkDeleted.
  • Every delivery.deleteBatchInterval (default 500ms) it flushes the accumulated batch (up to 1024 keys per flush): one Raft DeleteBatchCmd proposal in clustered mode — replicated so a new leader can't re-dispatch ACKed messages after failover — or a single storage batch in standalone mode.
  • Failed batches are re-queued and retried on the next flush (delete_failures_total tracks failures).
  • After a successful ACK flush, the hub releases tracking for the committed recipients, allowing the rebalance drain to proceed. The shared payload is deleted only after all required recipients complete. Successful explicit deletions clear tracking for the deleted keys.

docs.title: TTL janitor
docs.text: The dispatcher's inline TTL check only covers topics with live consumers. The janitor sweeps the entire database every delivery.ttlsweepInterval (default 60s), skips non-event keys (metadata, indexes), and routes expired messages to the deleter — so TTL messages with zero consumers still get cleaned up.

docs.title: Delivery guarantees
docs.text:
At-least-once

A message is re-dispatched if the consumer never ACKs (timeout), NACKs, or disconnects. Consumers must be idempotent. Duplicate delivery is also possible across a leader failover window in rare cases. There is no exactly-once mode and no per-message dedup at the consume path.

docs.title: Bounded full-message scheduler
docs.text: The dispatcher retains decoded StoredMessage data, including the payload. Storage remains authoritative; restarting discards and rebuilds the queue. Protocol messages, event keys, Raft commands, WAL/fsync settings, recipient ownership and at-least-once delivery are unchanged.

docs.title: Ownership and work
docs.text:
flowchart LR
  DB[(Storage)] --> D[Two bounded discovery workers]
  D -->|owned messages and cursor results| S[One scheduler: per-topic heaps and admission]
  S -->|due batches| P[Bounded preparation and delivery workers]
  P -->|outcome| S
  P --> Q[Existing bounded Hub queues and gRPC senders]
  R[One bounded permit-renewal worker] --> S
  P -->|prepare, quorum barrier, current receipt| DB

Only the scheduler changes heaps, admission counters, cursors, fair rotation, job markers and the deadline timer. Discovery workers receive copies of cursors, known keys and result reservations. There is at most one scan and one delivery job per topic. The two pools are independent, so a slow iterator or proposal on one topic does not stop another cached deadline. A topic cannot submit duplicate preparation jobs; known assigned keys are excluded from discovery and checked again when a result is admitted. Hub reservations remain the authority for individual recipient attempts after enqueue.

Delivery workers check permission before preparation, prepare under the existing context timeout, perform the post-preparation barrier, validate cached data, read the current receipt, recheck TTL/exact due time and enqueue through Hub. Actual gRPC Send and pointer-based attempt fencing stay in the existing sender. Read barriers grant permits from read start, as before. The legacy no-argument ReadBarrier hook captures its installation context: the preparation timeout does not cancel that hook. The production hook independently bounds reads to two seconds and uses the application cancellation context. Shutdown waits for it; custom hooks and storage calls must return before worker shutdown can complete. No scheduler/tracker lock spans storage, quorum or network work.

A single global message heap was rejected because a blocked topic could obstruct other topics. Per-topic heaps and fair rotation retain current one-job-per-topic semantics without another ownership partition. By default two discovery workers provide cross-topic isolation on both engines without overlapping scans of a topic. delivery.discoveryWorkers configures this pool from 1 to 16 workers. Separate per-topic scanner goroutines or scheduler partitions would add resident state and require evidence of a scheduler bottleneck first.

docs.title: Payload ownership and validity proof
docs.text:
Default proto.Unmarshal copies bytes into an independently allocated message. The vendored protobuf consumeBytes uses append(emptyBuf[:], v...); iterator memory is never retained. Topic strings and unknown fields are also decoded into owned data. No code mutates a retained message. Hub creates distinct queue-message pointers per attempt while sharing immutable payload bytes. Serialised values are released with the iterator, rather than cached alongside decoded messages.

Both built-in engines implement optional storage.CachedIterator. A token records an engine identity, a bounded hash slot of the event key, and the sequence captured before opening the engine snapshot. storage.payloadCacheSlots sets the number of version slots and pending counts per engine (default 4096, power of two from 64 to 1048576). The count is fixed when opening the engine and requires restart to change; both engines and both standalone/Raft use it. Slot indexes are uint32, and hashing uses a mask because the count is a power of two. Every batch that touches 24-byte event keys lazily allocates an S/8-byte bitmap; metadata-only batches allocate none. Repeated keys and collisions set the same bit, requiring no sorting. Both commit passes check S/64 words and visit their set bits. storage.payloadCacheHash selects fnv (FNV-1a 64-bit, default) or xxhash64 (XXH64) once at DB open, with the same hash used for token creation and mutations. Changing it requires restart and changes only local collision patterns, not stored event keys or the wire format. No bitmap pool is used. Before committing any such batch, under a short tracker lock, it advances the sequence, stamps affected slots and marks them pending. After storage commit returns (including failure), it advances/stamps again and clears its pending counts. Tracker locks never cover the commit itself. Multiple overlapping commits are supported by per-slot counts.

A token validates only when its slot is not pending and its last mutation sequence is no later than the token's snapshot sequence. Therefore:

  1. A mutation after snapshot capture invalidates the token before it changes DB contents. A mutation overlapping capture either remains pending at validation or has a completion sequence newer than capture. Neither can validate.
  2. Both Set and Delete participate, covering normal publish, replay, overwrite, explicit deletion, TTL, final ACK deletion and snapshot clear/repopulation. Recovery uses the same batch APIs, including its intermediate clear commit.
  3. Metadata-only preparation/partial ACK updates do not invalidate payloads. Hash collisions invalidate conservatively and require a fresh payload read.
  4. Future admission rejects invalidated speculative results. Due admission retains uncertain proofs for worker validation: an invalid token can reflect a hash collision or pending mutation rather than a changed message. Before committing a new receipt, the worker rereads an invalid/unsupported payload and checks its current exact due time and TTL. Eligible messages prepare on that attempt; deleted, expired or future replacements cannot freeze recipients. Built-in engines return refreshed bytes with a proof captured before the Get; preparation retains both the decoded message and that proof. Final delivery independently validates it or rereads after the read barrier. Unsupported engines and wrappers retain the conservative ordinary-Get fallback.
  5. A successful token validation is the payload freshness point corresponding to the old final Get. A delete starting afterwards can race enqueue just as it could after that Get; the change does not claim atomic delivery versus delete. A delete completed before validation cannot be bypassed by cached data.

The final receipt is read again after the barrier. Committed recipient ACK bits and receipt replacement are authoritative, even if preparation returned an older manifest. Missing or mismatched receipts do not send. Exact due/TTL checks and current Hub ownership/permit checks remain mandatory. No async delete notification is needed for cache safety; correctness lives at the storage mutation boundary. There is no new wire record or persistent version metadata.

docs.title: Admission, cursors and retries
docs.text:
Every normal due candidate uses the same admission and heap selection logic, including when either future-preload setting is zero. The synchronous test adapter uses those same functions. It is not a second sender algorithm.

A scan reserves result slots before dispatch. Future reservations plus retained future entries never exceed preloadMaxMessages. Due discovery has a separate allowance of max(discoveryWorkers, prepareWorkers) * prepareBatchSize, so future entries cannot exclude overdue arrivals. Assigned jobs have the existing prepareWorkers * prepareBatchSize bound. A heap pop clears its backing slot; sparse heaps/maps rebuild at one-quarter occupancy, bounding capacity by a constant factor. Topic removal clears its data and atomically invalidates its generation. Old scan results are admitted only to the original topic object; old delivery outcomes release only that object's job. Epoch checks and Hub fencing also cover unsubscribe/re-subscribe and rebalance.

Due and future scans have independent cyclic cursors. The scheduler acknowledges cursor advancement with the matching generation's result. Byte/size rejection preserves a resume key; iteration errors/exhaustion wrap to the beginning. Rejected admission, stale results, keys skipped while assigned and insertions behind a cursor are recovered by a subsequent cyclic pass. A cursor is never a completion watermark or proof of cache completeness.

Only results that actually enter admission trigger immediate refill, subject to reservations and fair rotation. A nonempty scan whose entries are stale, duplicated or unusable waits for the poll cadence. Due repair scans keep the poll cadence. Exhausted speculative future scans with no new candidates back off exponentially up to delivery.preloadScanIdleMaxInterval (default 100ms, zero disables backoff; the effective limit is at least the poll interval). Payload commit revisions reset this backoff on the next scheduler pass. Engines or wrappers without revision tracking keep the original poll cadence. A due-only scan does not change the future cursor. Each topic may retain/reserve at most one due batch, including while its preparation job is busy. The global due allowance covers at least every preparation worker, so busy topics cannot consume all admission while another worker is idle. A scan reserves only the unfilled part of its topic's batch allowance. Future-only scans can still refill within the independent future allowance; they reserve no shared due credits and do not advance the due cursor. Topics backing off release remaining ready entries, and a repair generation prevents older scan results from overwriting that rewind. A scan already in flight when backoff starts releases its due result rather than stranding credits; its future entries can still enter the separate cache. This also preserves admission with more delivery workers than discovery workers.

An individual recipient command that cannot fit the preparation-byte limit is logged, counted as delivery_rejected_total{reason="prepare_bytes"}, and waits at least one poll interval before rediscovery. Its other due entries also release shared credits while waiting; future entries retain their separate cache charge. Full queues, failed proposals and lost permission evict the assigned cache reference and wait at least one poll interval before retrying. Durable storage and current Hub readiness then drive recovery; a send-start ACK-deadline extension cannot be shortened by a cached retry timer. Unfinished fan-out interests remain independent in persisted receipts. No completed key history grows without bound.

Commit hints and per-message retry timers are omitted. Cyclic scans run on every serving replica, recover failed/missed arrivals without callback overflow, and recheck Hub state for NACK/timeout/full-queue recovery. Productive refill avoids the fixed polling throughput ceiling. The evaluation reports remaining repeated scan work; hints may be justified for larger databases or idle-topic populations, but would add apply-path metadata queues, overflow repair generations and hint-resolution reads. A key-only hint does not itself save payload I/O. No callbacks are installed on publish/apply, so failed commits cannot authorize cached arrivals.

The timer selects eligible topic heads, excluding busy topics and respecting retry eligibility. An earlier admitted deadline rearms it. Expired permission, full workers and unavailable recipients wait for an event or bounded retry deadline. Maintenance receipt processing shares bounded discovery/preparation slots with fair rotation, without adding inactive topics to the delivery heap.

docs.title: Count sizing and resource budget
docs.text:
The new default is 512 future messages, reduced from the metadata-only 4096. Speculative lookahead defaults to zero (opt-in), because the local many-topic and immediate cases do not meet the performance acceptance criteria. Existing explicit nonzero counts keep their meaning, but now retain full messages; operators should size them for actual payloads. The suggested opt-in trial is 512 at 100 ms, with both zero settings still supporting due-only delivery. Existing explicitly configured lookaheads are honoured. This is a count limit, not a hard byte cap.

On this arm64 build StoredMessage is 128 bytes and a candidate is 72 bytes. Allow roughly 512 bytes per retained message for decoded objects, strings, heap capacity slack and map bookkeeping. Payload allocation classes matter: 100 KiB rounds up to approximately 104 KiB here. At 512 future messages:

Payload Payload only Estimated future cache including overhead 1 KiB 0.5 MiB 0.75 MiB 64 KiB 32 MiB 32.25 MiB 100 KiB 50 MiB about 52.25 MiB with allocator rounding

The default receive limit is 100 KiB for the entire request, so usable payloads are smaller than that default envelope. It is configurable, and internal storage can contain larger valid messages. None are truncated or permanently rejected by a byte cap. These memory figures are estimates, not universal maximums.

Let C=preloadMaxMessages, B=prepareBatchSize, W=prepareWorkers, D=discoveryWorkers, and Q be a consumer's configured channel capacity. With defaults C=512, B=64, W=2, D=2:

Stage Bound Payload ownership after handoff Retained/reserved future entries C across heaps, scans and result channels combined Immutable decoded message Due scan results and ready entries max(D,W)B combined, independent of C; at most B retained/reserved per topic Same admission representation Assigned preparation/delivery jobs WB total; one/topic References removed from heap and held by worker Scanner transients At most D current decodes plus engine iterators Released on iterator close/job return Maintenance At most D discovery jobs and one pending receipt chunk; uses shared pools One transient payload read/decode per scanner, no retained payload batch Retry state Per-active-topic deadline and cyclic cursor; no retry payload side queue Failed jobs evict, then rediscover Heap/map backing capacity Heap <4 times live entries after drain; maps rebuilt with it Popped slots zeroed; removed topics clear arrays/maps Sender queues and tracked attempts Per consumer: Q buffered + at most max(1024,Q) records Shared immutable payload; expired buffered attempts may outlive tracking Delete/ACK buffers Existing 8192-key limits per completion kind Keys/recipient metadata, no payload cache Validity metadata At S configured slots, about 12*S bytes per engine plus an S/8-byte bitmap per batch touching message keys; defaults: 48 KiB and 512 bytes. Small snapshot token. No per-key unbounded history; commit traversal checks S/64 words and their set bits Known-key scan filters At most D copies of relevant bounded heap/assigned key sets Keys only

Conservatively, the heap/discovery/worker stages retain at most C+max(D,W)B+WB=768 message allocations plus current decoder transients. At 64 KiB this is about 48 MiB of payload plus bookkeeping, before sender queues, in-flight consumers, storage caches, publish batches and transient fallback reads. Fan-out shares the same allocation when enqueueing a worker's payload; count shared allocations once. A later rediscovered retry can allocate another copy while an expired sender queue still references the old one; the queue bounds above account for that separately.

docs.title: Prometheus metrics
docs.text:
Metrics are exposed in Prometheus format at observability.metrics.listen (default 0.0.0.0:9090). The metrics server starts before Raft so it can serve readiness/liveness probes during a slow bootstrap.

All application metric names below have the futureq_ prefix. Duration and lateness histograms use milliseconds.

docs.title: Publishing
docs.text:
Metric Type Labels Meaning publish_requests_total counter topic, ackLevel, result (rejected\|error\|success) Publish batches by outcome. Rejections include ack-level violations. messages_published_total counter topic Individual messages persisted publish_batch_size histogram — Messages per publish batch publish_latency_ms histogram — End-to-end publish latency raft_propose_duration_ms histogram ackLevel Raft proposal latency per ack level

Note

Batches may span topics; the topic label joins distinct topics with |.

docs.title: Delivery
docs.text:
Metric Type Labels Meaning messages_dispatched_total counter topic, group_id Successful handoffs to sender queues, once per recipient; includes retries. messages_in_flight gauge topic, group_id Active delivery attempts, including queued sends and successful ACKs awaiting persistence. Each group/key counts once; each universal recipient/key counts separately. dispatch_pass_duration_ms histogram — Successful preparation results processed through queueing, timed from candidate collection start; excludes speculative preload work and waiting for due time. Not a full topic pass. delivery_latency_ms histogram topic Legacy enqueue-to-candidate-selection age, observed for successfully queued messages. Includes intentional producer delay; excludes preparation and sender-queue waiting. delivery_overhead_ms histogram topic Candidate-selection-start time minus scheduled due time, clamped at zero, observed for successfully queued messages. Includes both live and cached selection. delivery_sender_enqueue_lateness_ms histogram topic Actual sender-enqueue time minus the individual due time, per successfully queued recipient attempt. Includes preparation; excludes sender-queue waiting. delivery_send_lateness_ms histogram topic Time immediately before each authorized gRPC Send attempt minus the individual due time. Includes sender-queue waiting, retries, and failed send attempts. delivery_grpc_sends_total counter topic Successful gRPC sends, including retries and fan-out. Not client acknowledgements. delivery_queue_depth gauge queue consumer: queued sender attempts across local subscriptions; prepare: outstanding jobs, not messages; preload: retained full-message entries charged to the future allowance, including overdue or stale entries; ready: due-scan entries waiting in heaps; discovery: outstanding scan jobs/results. Ready entries exclude assigned preparation jobs. Not persistent backlog. delivery_oldest_queued_lateness_ms gauge — Oldest unsent tracked attempt's lateness, sampled by the scheduler. Excludes preload candidates. delivery_oldest_preparation_lateness_ms gauge — Oldest candidate due time in outstanding preparation jobs, sampled after scheduling. Zero when no due preparation job remains. delivery_scan_duration_ms histogram — Aggregate local duration of bounded collection operations across all four paths below, including empty operations. Excludes read barriers, preparation, and time resident in the preload cache. delivery_collection_duration_ms histogram path Duration by due_scan, maintenance, preload_scan, or preload_ready. preload_ready is cached candidate selection, before preparation. delivery_scanned_keys_total counter — Event-key observations in live and speculative preload storage scans, including repeated reads. Excludes cache-only selection and maintenance receipt scans. delivery_ownership_filtered_total counter — Event-key observations rejected for having no local owner, in live or speculative preload storage scans. delivery_candidates_total counter source (scan\|preload) Due candidates selected for preparation, including retries. Excludes future loads and maintenance. source="preload" counts cached candidate hits, not successful deliveries. delivery_preload_capacity gauge — Configured maximum future-message entries on this node. Due work has a separate bounded allowance. Zero when preloading is disabled or the scheduler stops. delivery_preload_loaded_total counter — New full-message entries loaded into reserved future discovery/cache slots; known-key scans do not increment it. A stale result can be rejected before heap admission. Reloading after invalidation counts again. delivery_preload_scanned_keys_total counter — Speculative preload event-key observations; a subset of delivery_scanned_keys_total, not additional work to sum with it. messages_expired_total counter topic, source (dispatcher\|janitor) Accepted TTL deletion requests on this node, attributed to the source that queued each request. Repeated scans and failed flush retries are deduplicated while a deletion is pending. Not committed deletes or globally unique messages. active_consumers gauge topic, group_id Connected consumers consumer_ack_total counter topic, group_id, success ACK/NACK frames received delete_batch_size histogram — Keys per delete flush delete_failures_total counter — Failed delete flushes (retried)

The full-message scheduler adds these bounded-label metrics. Storage scans and heap selection stay in the existing duration series; do not sum a subset with its aggregate. The cache counters describe validation, not successful sends.

Metric (prefix futureq_) Type Labels Meaning delivery_prepare_payload_cache_total counter source (cache, fallback) Preparation payload validations; fallback counts full payload Get attempts, including missing, expired or not-yet-due messages. These attempts are excluded from the final-delivery cache-hit ratio. delivery_payload_cache_total counter source (cache, fallback) Final payload validations using retained data or a fresh read fallback. delivery_payload_reads_total counter — Final-delivery payload Get calls. Preparation existence reads and maintenance payload reads are separate storage work, excluded here. delivery_payload_decodes_total counter stage (discovery, preparation, delivery) Full-message decode attempts in normal discovery, preparation fallback or final delivery fallback. Excludes maintenance receipt repair. delivery_discovery_bytes_total counter — Key/value bytes examined in due/future discovery, including known keys and filtered keys. A scan observation is counted once; not physical device bytes. delivery_repair_scans_total counter — Bounded cyclic due passes, including startup/ordinary discovery, late-arrival and retry repair. delivery_worker_outcomes_total counter outcome (queued, not-ready, permission-lost, prepare-failed) Delivery job outcomes. queued means at least one message enqueued, not a gRPC send or committed ACK. Zero-send work remains recoverable.

delivery_rejected_total{reason="prepare_bytes"} counts a candidate whose current recipient command cannot fit even an empty preparation batch. Selection logs the byte limit and topic; the scheduler backs off before rediscovery. An unfit command is not a successful preparation or send, and its payload stays in storage.

Scheduler design and resource bounds describes payload validity, current-receipt reads, retry recovery and count-based sizing.

docs.title: Interpreting preloading and readiness
docs.text:
Loading a future key is not a send attempt. It changes preload occupancy and load counters, but does not change sender-enqueue lateness, send lateness, dispatch counts, or in-flight records. Preparation, due-time checks, ownership, TTL checks, and delivery permissions still apply before queueing.

Use delivery_sender_enqueue_lateness_ms to measure when a message becomes ready for its sender, and delivery_send_lateness_ms for lateness immediately before the gRPC send. The legacy selection-time histograms exclude preparation and must not be described as end-to-end delivery latency. Percentiles are independently sampled; subtracting stage percentiles does not measure stage time.

The aggregate collection histogram now includes preload scanning and cached selection. For comparisons across this change, use the path histogram to separate work; a lower live-scan rate alone does not establish lower total cost. Gauges are node-local snapshots updated at scheduler boundaries. A retained preload entry includes an owned decoded payload and can be future-due or stale, so occupancy is not a count of messages currently authorized to send.

For example, preload occupancy as a fraction of enabled capacity is:

futureq_delivery_queue_depth{queue="preload"}
  / ignoring(queue) (futureq_delivery_preload_capacity > 0)

The fraction of selected candidates supplied by preloading is:

sum(rate(futureq_delivery_candidates_total{source="preload"}[5m]))
  / (sum(rate(futureq_delivery_candidates_total[5m])) > 0)

These measure cache usage, not delivery success or a traditional cache-lookup hit ratio. Apply matching job/pod filters when querying a shared Prometheus.

docs.title: Logging
docs.text: Structured logging via zap; level configurable with observability.logging.level (default info) or FUTUREQ_OBSERVABILITY_LOGGING_LEVEL.

docs.title: Repository structure
docs.text:
futureq/
├── cmd/futureq/            # Cobra CLI (start, leave)
├── internal/
│   ├── main.go              # entrypoint
│   ├── app/                 # wiring: storage, repositories, Raft lifecycle
│   ├── api/grpc/            # gRPC server + handlers (producer, consumer, cluster)
│   ├── config/              # config loading + env overrides + validation
│   ├── dispatcher/          # scan/dispatch loop, hub, deleter, TTL janitor
│   ├── metrics/             # Prometheus server
│   ├── raft/
│   │   ├── event/           # event-shard state machine & binary commands
│   │   └── leaderpersist/   # LogDB decorator + tracker for leader acks
│   ├── repository/          # event repository abstraction
│   └── storage/             # Pebble & bbolt engines behind a common contract
├── pkg/
│   ├── raft/metadata/       # metadata-group Raft (public: cluster membership)
│   ├── log/                 # zap logger setup
│   └── utils/               # 24-byte event key helpers
├── config.example.yaml      # documented defaults
├── Dockerfile
└── CHANGELOG.md

pkg/raft/metadata is deliberately public so external SDKs can join the metadata group as read-only observers and receive live topology updates.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
go build ./...       # build
go test ./...        # run tests (CI runs with -race)
golangci-lint run    # lint

docs.title: CI (GitHub Actions, on every push)
docs.text:
Workflow What it runs build.yml go mod download + go build -v ./... test.yml go test -race -v ./... golangci-lint.yml golangci-lint action (latest version, read-only permissions)

All on ubuntu-latest with Go 1.27.1, read from go.mod.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Contributions are welcome — please open an issue to discuss substantial changes before sending a PR. FutureQ is released under the MIT license.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Go 1.27.1+
  • (Optional) Docker

docs.title: Build & run a standalone node
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/futureq-io/futureq.git
cd futureq
go build -o futureq ./cmd/futureq

cp config.example.yaml config.yaml   # adjust as needed
./futureq start -c config.yaml

A standalone node (cluster.enabled: false) writes directly to Pebble with a synchronous fsync per publish batch — perfect for local development. See the gRPC API page for how to talk to it.

docs.title: Run a 3-node cluster
docs.text:
On the first node, enable clustering and list its bootstrap member. Use addresses that other nodes and clients can reach:

api:
  grpc:
    advertise: "10.0.0.1:8443"
cluster:
  enabled: true
  nodeId: 1
  shardId: 1
  raft:
    advertise: "10.0.0.1:50005"
    initialMembers:
      1: "10.0.0.1:50005"

For each additional node, give it a unique cluster.nodeId, its own api.grpc.advertise and cluster.raft.advertise, and a seed address. For example, node 2 uses:

api:
  grpc:
    advertise: "10.0.0.2:8443"
cluster:
  enabled: true
  nodeId: 2
  raft:
    advertise: "10.0.0.2:50005"
  joinSeeds:
    - "10.0.0.1:8443"

The --join flag overrides cluster.joinSeeds for one start:

./futureq start -c node2.yaml --join 10.0.0.1:8443
./futureq start -c node3.yaml --join 10.0.0.1:8443

Join flow

On first start the joining node contacts each seed until one accepts its JoinCluster request. Membership is registered on both the event shard and the metadata group — first as a non-voting member that catches up, then promoted to voter. Restarts detect local Raft data and skip the join flow automatically. cluster.raft.initialMembers and cluster.joinSeeds cannot both be set in a config file.

docs.title: Docker
docs.text:
docker build -t futureq .
docker run -p 8443:8443 -p 9090:9090 -p 50005:50005 \
  -v $(pwd)/config.yaml:/app/config.yaml \
  futureq start -c /app/config.yaml

docs.title: The storage contract
docs.text:
All engines implement the storage.DB interface (internal/storage/contract.go): Get, atomic Batch (Set/Delete + commit with sync mode), and ordered iteration via NewIter / Scan(opts, yield). The contract requires:

  • Lexicographic byte ordering of the whole keyspace — the dispatch and TTL logic depends on range scans.
  • ErrNotFound sentinel error.
  • Lower bound inclusive, upper bound exclusive.
  • Yielded key/value slices are valid only inside the yield call — callers copy what they keep.

Because of this contract, the dispatcher and janitor are completely engine-agnostic.

docs.title: The 24-byte event key
docs.text:
Every message is stored under a 24-byte, big-endian, lexicographically sortable key (pkg/utils/keys.go):

Bytes Field Meaning 0..8 topicHash xxhash64 of the topic name 8..16 bucket Time bucket = fireAtMs / timeBucket, where fireAtMs = enqueuedAtMs + delayMs. With timeBucket = 0, raw milliseconds are used (max precision). 16..24 eventID Monotonic counter assigned by the event repository (durable across restarts)

The sort order is therefore topic → time bucket → ID, which makes "give me everything due for topic X before now" a single range scan between two computed bounds:

Helper Bound TopicLowerBound [topicHash] — inclusive TopicUpperBound [topicHash + 1] — exclusive DueUpperBound [topicHash][maxBucket + 1] — exclusive; future buckets are never scanned

The stored value is the protobuf StoredMessage (topic, payload, enqueue time, delay, TTL, indexes). The 24-byte key doubles as the opaque delivery_tag consumers receive and echo back on ACK.

docs.title: Pebble (default)
docs.text: LSM-tree engine (storage.pebble.*). Scans and iterators run on internal snapshots, so reads never block writes. Options: disk or in-memory mode (vfs.NewMem() — same code path, nothing persists, WAL auto-disabled), WAL toggle (auto-off in clustered mode — the Raft log is the WAL), block cache (default 16MiB) and memtable size (default 64MiB).

docs.title: bbolt
docs.text: Alternative single-file engine (storage.engine: bolt). One flat B+-tree bucket preserves the ordered keyspace. Reads use read-only transactions; scans run inside a single db.View with cursor seek/next. Batches are buffered and applied in one db.Update, which always fsyncs on commit — the sync-mode flag is ignored and Flush is a no-op.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text: Not a separate engine: it's Pebble in mode: memory. Ephemeral workloads only.

docs.title: Event repository
docs.text:
internal/repository/events.go sits between handlers/state machine and storage:

  • Assigns monotonic event IDs — leader-only in Raft mode; the last ID is persisted under metadata/event-repo/last-id (big-endian uint64) so restarts never reuse IDs. Replicas advance past applied IDs via ObserveID instead of assigning.
  • Constructs the 24-byte keys and writes optional secondary indexes (proto-marshaled index payloads pointing back to the key).
